✅ Correct Answer: CH4, CO2, N2, H2S, H2

question: A bioremediation mesocosm experiment has been carried out on a plot with 250 ppm aromatic molecules as contaminants. After 15 days the level of aromatic molecules came down to 100 ppm at a temperature of 48 ± 2°C. The electrical conductance of this site has increased over time because of the
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Electrical Conductivity during Bioremediation:
  • As aerobic/anaerobic microorganisms metabolize neutral aromatic hydrocarbons into polar, charged metabolites (such as short-chain organic acids, catechols, and acetate), free ionic species accumulate in the soil pore water.
  • This buildup of charged ions increases the overall electrical conductance of the mesocosm.
✅ Correct Answer: Increase in organic acids

question: Internal coordinates for representation of the three-dimensional structure of a protein consists of:
options: bond lengths, bond angles and dihedral angles
Cartesian coordinates X, Y and Z for all the atoms
spherical polar coordinates R, θ, Φ for all atoms
correct_answer: bond lengths, bond angles and dihedral angles
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Internal Coordinates in Molecular Modeling:
  • In computational chemistry, molecular geometry can be described using Cartesian coordinates ($x, y, z$) or internal coordinates (Z-matrix).
  • Internal coordinates define the relative positions of atoms without translational or rotational degrees of freedom, consisting of:
    1. Bond lengths ($r$)
    2. Bond angles ($\theta$)
    3. Dihedral (torsion) angles ($\phi, \psi, \omega$)
✅ Correct Answer: bond lengths, bond angles and dihedral angles

question: Cis-peptide unit corresponds to the O-C-N-H dihedral angle (degrees) of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cis vs Trans Peptide Bond Dihedral Angle ($\omega$):
  • The peptide bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, keeping the four atoms ($ ext{C}_\alpha - \text{C} - \text{N} - \text{C}_\alpha$ or $\text{O}-\text{C}-\text{N}-\text{H}$) in a planar conformation.
  • Trans-conformation: The carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen are on opposite sides; the $\omega$ dihedral angle is $180^\circ$.
  • Cis-conformation: The carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen are on the same side; the $\omega$ dihedral angle is $0^\circ$.
✅ Correct Answer: 0

question: Which of the following corresponds to the amino acid pair having maximum and minimum number of allowed conformations in the Ramachandran plot?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ramachandran Plot Allowed Conformations:
  • Glycine (Max): Has only a single hydrogen atom as its side chain (no bulky $\beta$-carbon), experiencing virtually no steric hindrance $implies$ displays the maximum allowed conformational space on the Ramachandran plot ($>60\%$ of plot area).
  • Proline (Min): Has a rigid five-membered pyrrolidine ring that locks the backbone dihedral angle $\phi$ at approximately $-65^\circ \pm 15^\circ$, severely restricting allowed conformations $implies$ displays the minimum allowed area.
✅ Correct Answer: Max: Gly, Min: Pro

question: If the energy of a protein structure is calculated using molecular mechanics forcefield, which of the following energy components CANNOT have a negative value?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Molecular Mechanics Force Fields:
  • In molecular mechanics (e.g. AMBER, CHARMM, GROMOS), the total potential energy is the sum of bonded and non-bonded terms: $$E_{\text{total}} = E_{\text{bonded}} + E_{\text{non-bonded}}$$ where bonded terms include bond stretching (bond energy), angle bending, and torsional energy, modeled using harmonic potentials ($k_b(r - r_0)^2$).
✅ Correct Answer: Bond energy

question: X, Y and Z correspond to three different conformers of an 18-residue peptide, where X: α helix, Y: β strand and Z: 310 helix. Which of the following correspond to the conformers in the decreasing order of end to end distance?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] End-to-End Distance of Peptide Conformations:
  • For an 18-residue peptide:
    • $\beta$-strand (Y): Fully extended polypeptide chain with an axial rise of $\approx 3.4 - 3.8\text{ \AA}$ per residue $implies$ longest end-to-end distance ($L \approx 65\text{ \AA}$).
    • $3_{10}$-helix (Z): Tighter, more elongated helix than $\alpha$-helix, with a pitch of $6.0\text{ \AA}$ and axial rise of $\approx 2.0\text{ \AA}$ per residue $implies$ intermediate distance.
    • $\alpha$-helix (X): Compact helix with $3.6$ residues per turn and an axial rise of only $1.5\text{ \AA}$ per residue $implies$ shortest end-to-end distance ($L = 18 \times 1.5 = 27\text{ \AA}$).
  • Decreasing order of end-to-end distance: $\mathbf{Y > Z > X}$.
✅ Correct Answer: Y, Z, X

question: Which one of the following protein structure prediction methods is based on the principle of locating lowest energy minimum in the conformation space of a protein?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ab Initio Protein Structure Prediction:
  • Comparative (homology) modeling and threading (fold recognition) require homologous template structures from the PDB.
  • When no suitable homologous template exists in structural databases, tertiary structure must be predicted directly from the amino acid sequence from first principles using physics-based force fields and conformational sampling. This method is called Ab initio (de novo) protein structure prediction.
✅ Correct Answer: Ab initio structure prediction

question: Which one of the following can be used to measure the extent of similarity between the predicted structure of a protein and its experimentally determined structure?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD):
  • RMSD (Root Mean Square Deviation) is the standard quantitative measure used to compare the structural similarity of two superimposed protein 3D structures: $$\text{RMSD} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{r}_i^A - \mathbf{r}_i^B\|^2}$$ where $\mathbf{r}_i$ are the coordinates of the $C_\alpha$ atoms. Lower RMSD indicates higher structural identity.
✅ Correct Answer: Root mean square deviation (RMSD)

question: The PROSITE pattern representing the conserved sequence motif for a new family of AMP binding protein is [LIVMFY]-X(2)-[STG]-[STAG]-G-[ST]. You are given a sequence of a 15-amino acid stretch starting from the first residue of the motif. Which one of the following proteins is likely to have AMP binding function?

question: Dot matrix analysis of the amino acid sequences of lambda phage cI (horizontal sequence) and phage P22 c2 (vertical sequence) repressors is shown below. Which one of the following is correct?
options: Line A indicates similar sequences and Line B indicates repeat sequences

question: An alignment of two protein sequences showing matches, mismatches and gaps (Δ) is given below: Sequence A: A G A Δ C D E V I G Sequence B: A G E Y C D Δ V I G The similarity score (%) for the above alignment will be:
explanation:

  • Given alignment:
    • Seq A: A G A Δ C D E V I G
    • Seq B: A G E Y C D Δ V I G
  • Total aligned columns = 10.
  • Examining the 10 positions:
    • Col 1: A/A (Match, 1)
    • Col 2: G/G (Match, 1)
    • Col 3: A/E (Mismatch)
    • Col 4: Δ/Y (Gap)
    • Col 5: C/C (Match, 1)
    • Col 6: D/D (Match, 1)
    • Col 7: E/Δ (Gap)
    • Col 8: V/V (Match, 1)
    • Col 9: I/I (Match, 1)
    • Col 10: G/G (Match, 1)
  • Total matches = 7 out of 10 positions $\implies$ Similarity score = $\frac{7}{10} \times 100\% = 70\%$.
✅ Correct Answer: 70

question: Which one of the following is a depiction of the standard GenBank sequence entry format?
options: FASTA format (>YCZ2_YEAST protein in HMR 3' region...)
Legacy sequence header format (BASE COUNT 215 A 224 G 263 G 250 T ORIGIN...)
NBRF/PIR format (>P1; ILEC lexA repressor - Escherichia coli...)
GenBank flatfile format (LOCUS, DEFINITION, ACCESSION, KEYWORDS, SOURCE, FEATURES, ORIGIN //)
correct_answer: GenBank flatfile format (LOCUS, DEFINITION, ACCESSION, KEYWORDS, SOURCE, FEATURES, ORIGIN //)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] GenBank Flatfile Format Characteristics:
  • A standard NCBI GenBank sequence record flatfile consists of:
    • Header lines beginning with predefined uppercase tags: LOCUS, DEFINITION, ACCESSION, VERSION, KEYWORDS, SOURCE, ORGANISM, REFERENCE.
    • The FEATURES table detailing coding sequences (CDS), genes, promoters.
    • The sequence itself starting after ORIGIN, numbered with 60 bases per line separated into 10-base blocks, terminating with a double slash (//).
✅ Correct Answer: GenBank flatfile format (LOCUS, DEFINITION, ACCESSION, KEYWORDS, SOURCE, FEATURES, ORIGIN //)

question: Two sequences of comparable length have several regions that align locally, but are separated by other regions that align poorly. Which algorithm can be used to find the highest-scoring alignment between the two sequences?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Global Alignment Algorithms:
  • When two sequences are of comparable length across their entire extent, global alignment algorithms are employed to find the optimal end-to-end alignment.
  • The standard dynamic programming algorithm for global sequence alignment is the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm.
✅ Correct Answer: Needleman-Wunch algorithm

question: A sample genetic code is given below: Amino Acid: Pro | Val | Gly | His | Asp | Tyr | Thr | Lys Codon: CCN | GUN | GGN | CAY | GAY | UAY | CAN | AAR If an amino acid substitution matrix based on genetic code is derived for sequence alignment and analysis from evolutionary studies, which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Pro is most similar to His
Pro is most similar to Thr
Gly is most similar to Lys
Asp is most similar to Thr
correct_answer: Pro is most similar to Thr
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetic Code Distance & Amino Acid Substitution:
  • Codon for Proline (Pro): $\text{CCN}$
  • Codon for Threonine (Thr): $\text{CAN}$
  • Notice that Pro (CCN) and Thr (CAN) differ by only a single nucleotide at the second codon position ($ ext{C} \leftrightarrow \text{A}$), meaning they can mutate into each other via a single point mutation. None of the other listed pairs can interconvert with a single substitution.
  • Thus, based on the genetic code matrix, Pro is most similar to Thr.
✅ Correct Answer: Pro is most similar to Thr

question: Which one of the following tools can reliably establish an evolutionary link between two proteins and align them even if they share very low degree of sequence similarity?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Iterative Profile-Based Sequence Searching (PSI-BLAST):
  • PSI-BLAST (Position-Specific Iterated BLAST) builds a Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (PSSM) from initial BLAST hits and iteratively queries the database with this profile.
  • Because PSSMs capture conserved sequence motifs and variable positions across families, PSI-BLAST can reliably detect remote evolutionary homologs that share very low overall sequence similarity ("twilight zone", $<25\%$ identity) which standard pairwise BLAST fails to find.
✅ Correct Answer: PSI-BLAST

question: Of the two databases A and B, the database A is larger in size than database B. In a BLAST search, a sequence has a highly significant match with the same entry in both the databases. Which of the following is TRUE?
options: Match in Database A will have lower E-value when compared to Database B
Match in Database B will have lower E-value when compared to Database A
The E-value will be same for both the matches
The E-value cannot be compared for such a search
correct_answer: Match in Database B will have lower E-value when compared to Database A
explanation:
[CONCEPT] E-value Dependence on Database Size:
  • The Expect value ($E$) of a database alignment score $S$ is given by: $$E = K \cdot m \cdot N \cdot e^{-\lambda S}$$ where $m$ is query length and $N$ is total database size (total letters/sequences).
  • $E$ is directly proportional to database size $N$.
  • Since Database B is smaller than Database A ($N_B < N_A$), an alignment with the same raw score will yield a lower (more statistically significant) E-value in Database B.
✅ Correct Answer: Match in Database B will have lower E-value when compared to Database A

question: Parents who appear normal have a child with sickle cell anemia, which is an autosomal recessive trait. The woman becomes pregnant again and is told that she is carrying fraternal twins. What is the probability that both the twins will develop sickle cell anemia?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Autosomal Recessive Inheritance & Fraternal Twins:
  • Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder ($ss$).
  • Normal parents who have an affected child must both be obligate heterozygotes ($Ss \times Ss$).
  • For each pregnancy, the probability of an offspring inheriting the disease ($ss$) is $\frac{1}{4}$.
  • Fraternal (dizygotic) twins arise from two separate eggs fertilized by two separate sperm. Their genetic inheritances are independent events: $$P(\text{both twins affected}) = P(\text{twin 1 affected}) \times P(\text{twin 2 affected}) = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{16}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 1/16

question: The following pedigree shows the inheritance of a human disease. What is the most likely mode of inheritance for this trait and what is the probability that a son of III 1 would be affected by the disease, if III 1 is known to be a carrier.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] X-Linked Recessive Pedigree Probability:
  • Pedigree analysis demonstrates classic sex-linked (X-linked) recessive inheritance (mostly males affected, transmission through unaffected carrier females).
  • If female III-1 is known to be a carrier ($X^A X^a$):
    • She passes her abnormal $X^a$ allele to $50\%$ of her offspring.
    • For a son ($XY$), he inherits the $Y$ chromosome from the father and either $X^A$ or $X^a$ from the mother.
    • Therefore, the probability that a son of III-1 is affected ($X^a Y$) is $\frac{1}{2} = \mathbf{0.5}$.
✅ Correct Answer: Sex-linked recessive; 0.5

question: A 30 Kb candidate gene linked to prostate cancer from a patient was digested with XhoI. Following Southern hybridization of the digested products with the full-length gene probe, three bands of 15, 10 and 5 Kb sizes were obtained. However, an identical experiment in normal individuals gave a 15 Kb fragment. This could be due to:
options: Presence of SNP in the candidate gene
Deletion of a fragment of DNA from the candidate gene
The probe could not identify the 10 and 5 Kb fragments
The probe could only identify the 15 Kb fragment
correct_answer: Presence of SNP in the candidate gene
explanation:
[CONCEPT] RFLP and Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs):
  • In normal individuals, XhoI does not cut internally within the 15 Kb fragment, yielding a single 15 Kb hybridizing band on Southern blot.
  • In the cancer patient, three bands of 15, 10, and 5 Kb are observed ($10 + 5 = 15\text{ Kb}$).
  • This indicates the creation of a new XhoI restriction cleavage site ($5'-\text{CTCGAG}-3'$) on one allele via a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) / point mutation, cleaving the 15 Kb fragment into 10 Kb and 5 Kb fragments while the other homologous chromosome remains uncut (15 Kb).
✅ Correct Answer: Presence of SNP in the candidate gene

question: In a given population, 1 out of 400 individuals has cancer caused by a recessive allele ‘p’. Assuming the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the expected proportion of individuals who carry the ‘p’ allele but do not develop cancer?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium Carrier Frequency:
  • Given: Frequency of homozygous affected individuals ($q^2$): $$q^2 = \frac{1}{400} \implies q = \sqrt{\frac{1}{400}} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05$$
  • Frequency of normal allele ($p$): $$p = 1 - q = 1 - \frac{1}{20} = \frac{19}{20} = 0.95$$
  • Heterozygous carriers ($2pq$) carry the allele but do not develop cancer: $$2pq = 2 \times \left(\frac{19}{20}\right) \times \left(\frac{1}{20}\right) = \frac{38}{400}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 38/400

question: Color blindness in human beings is an X-linked trait. A color-blind man has a 45, X daughter who is also color-blind. The nondisjunction that leads to the 45, X daughter occurred in which parent and in which meiotic division?
options: Brother, father and mother; first meiotic division
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Turner Syndrome (45, X) & Nondisjunction Origin:
  • A color-blind man has genotype $X^c Y$ (where $X^c$ carries the recessive color-blindness allele).
  • His daughter has Turner syndrome ($45, X$) and is color-blind ($X^c$).
  • Because the father has only $X^c$ and $Y$:
    • If the daughter inherited her single $X$ chromosome from the father ($X^c$), she would be color-blind, which would mean the mother provided NO sex chromosome (nondisjunction in mother).
    • Nondisjunction during maternal meiosis leads to an egg lacking an X chromosome ($n-1 = 22, 0$), which when fertilized by the father's $X^c$ sperm produces a $45, X^c$ color-blind daughter.
✅ Correct Answer: Mother; first meiotic division

question: A marker present outside the targeted QTL used to check the crossing over is called:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Recombinant Selection in Marker-Assisted Backcrossing:
  • In marker-assisted backcrossing (MABC), two types of markers flanking the target QTL/gene are used:
    • Fore-ground selection: Selects for the presence of the donor target allele.
    • Recombinant selection: Uses markers outside but closely linked to the target QTL to select individuals where recombination occurred between the target QTL and the linked donor chromosome, thereby minimizing linkage drag (unwanted donor genome segments flanking the gene).
✅ Correct Answer: Recombinant marker

question: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay is:
options: Much rapid in out-crossing than in selfing species
Much rapid in selfing than in out-crossing species
Equal in selfing and out-crossing species
Not dependent on selfing or out-crossing
correct_answer: Much rapid in out-crossing than in selfing species
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) Decay:
  • Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) is the non-random association of alleles at different loci.
  • In out-crossing (cross-pollinating) species, frequent outcrossing and heterozygosity lead to extensive effective recombination events in every generation, breaking up ancestral haplotype blocks very rapidly.
  • In contrast, selfing species maintain high homozygosity, making recombination between homozygous loci genetically ineffective. Therefore, LD decay is much more rapid in out-crossing than in selfing species.
✅ Correct Answer: Much rapid in out-crossing than in selfing species

question: ‘Gene for gene’ hypothesis states that:
options: For each resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding gene for virulence in the pathogen conferring host resistance
For each resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding gene for avirulence in the pathogen conferring host resistance
For each resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding gene for aggressiveness in the pathogen conferring host resistance
For each resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding gene for non-aggressiveness in the pathogen conferring host resistance
correct_answer: For each resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding gene for avirulence in the pathogen conferring host resistance
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Flor's Gene-for-Gene Hypothesis:
  • Formulated by Harold Flor in 1942 based on studies of flax rust (Linum usitatissimum and Melampsora lini):
  • The hypothesis states that: For each gene conditioning resistance in the host plant, there is a corresponding specific gene conditioning avirulence in the pathogen.
  • Resistance occurs only when the host has a dominant resistance allele ($R$) and the pathogen has the corresponding dominant avirulence allele ($Avr$). Interaction between $R$ and $Avr$ products triggers the hypersensitive defense response.
✅ Correct Answer: For each resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding gene for avirulence in the pathogen conferring host resistance

question: In an ordered tetrad analysis, if the two genes are not linked, the ………… will be almost equal.
options: Parental ditype, non-parental ditype and tetratype
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Tetrad Analysis for Unlinked Genes:
  • In fungi (like Neurospora or yeast), when two genes are on different non-homologous chromosomes (unlinked):
  • Independent assortment produces:
    • Parental Ditype (PD) asci: contain only parental genotypes (e.g. $AB, AB, ab, ab$).
    • Non-Parental Ditype (NPD) asci: contain only recombinant genotypes (e.g. $Ab, Ab, aB, aB$).
  • Because alternate alignments of non-homologous chromosome pairs at Metaphase I are equally probable, the frequency of PD equals the frequency of NPD ($PD \approx NPD$).
✅ Correct Answer: Parental ditype and non-parental ditype

question: Assume that a marker M1 is present 5 cM away on one side of a gene “X” (a desirable allele of the gene), while marker M2 is present 10 cM away on the other side of the gene. The donor’s genotype is M1M1XXM2M2, while the recipient has m1m1xxm2m2 genotype. A cross was made between these two individuals. The F1 is crossed to recipient. The progeny of this cross had 1000 plants. How many plants from this progeny will have both the markers (M1 & M2) present while the desired gene is absent? (Assume no interference)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Coincidence and Double Crossover Frequency:
  • Given: Marker $M1$ is $5\text{ cM}$ ($r_1 = 0.05$) from gene, and $M2$ is $5\text{ cM}$ ($r_2 = 0.05$) on the other side.
  • Theoretical expected double crossover frequency = $0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.0025$ ($0.25\%$).
  • However, over very short genetic distances ($<10\text{ cM}$), complete positive chromosome interference ($I = 1$) prevents a second crossover from occurring near the first, reducing the observed double crossover frequency to 0.
✅ Correct Answer: 0

question: Maize transgenic for bacterial CspA (a RNA chaperone) imparts tolerance to:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cold Shock Protein A (CspA) & Drought/Water Stress:
  • Bacterial CspA (Cold shock protein A) functions as an RNA chaperone that unwinds secondary structures in mRNAs, facilitating translation under environmental stresses.
  • Transgenic maize plants expressing bacterial cold shock proteins (CspA/CspB) (e.g. Monsanto's DroughtGard maize) maintain protein translation and cellular function under severe water stress (drought), preserving grain yield.
✅ Correct Answer: Water stress

question: Assume gene “A” is dominant over “a” and “B1” is codominant over “B2” in petunia. A cross is made between two individuals – AAB1B2 x aaB1B2. Assuming that there is no gene interaction, the progeny will segregate in a phenotypic ratio of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Phenotypic Ratios with Codominance:
  • For gene $B$, where allele $B1$ is codominant with $B2$:
  • A cross between two heterozygotes ($B1B2 \times B1B2$) produces genotypes: $$1\text{ }B1B1 : 2\text{ }B1B2 : 1\text{ }B2B2$$
  • Because each genotype exhibits a distinct phenotype in codominance, the phenotypic ratio directly mirrors the genotypic ratio: 1:2:1.
✅ Correct Answer: 1:2:1

question: A multiline variety is:
options: a mixture of isogenic lines that usually confer resistance to a specific disease
a single genotype with stacked multiple genes conferring resistance to a specific disease
a mixture of pure lines having different traits
correct_answer: a mixture of isogenic lines that usually confer resistance to a specific disease
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Multiline Varieties in Plant Breeding:
  • A multiline variety is a composite mixture of several near-isogenic lines (NILs) that are agronomically identical (same height, maturity, flowering time) but differ in carrying distinct single resistance genes against specific pathogen races (e.g. against wheat rust).
  • This genetic heterogeneity slows down pathogen epidemics because any single pathogen race can only attack a fraction of the plants in the field.
✅ Correct Answer: a mixture of isogenic lines that usually confer resistance to a specific disease

question: A variety “X” is a donor for resistance to blast, but it has an undesirable gene for lodging susceptibility that is tightly linked to the blast resistant gene. The best breeding method which has high probability of breaking this linkage is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Backcross Breeding for Trait Introgression:
  • When a donor variety possesses a highly desirable trait (such as blast resistance) alongside undesirable agronomic characteristics:
  • The Backcross method is the method of choice. The donor is crossed with a well-adapted, high-yielding elite recipient variety (recurrent parent), and the progeny are repeatedly backcrossed to the recurrent parent while selecting for blast resistance. This recovers $>99\%$ of the recurrent parent's elite genome while retaining the resistance gene.
✅ Correct Answer: Backcross method

question: Upon application of the inhibitor, DBMIB (Dibromothymoquinone) which one of the following events in the chloroplast electron transport chain will NOT take place?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] DBMIB Inhibition in Photosynthetic Electron Transport:
  • DBMIB (2,5-dibromo-3-methyl-6-isopropyl-p-benzoquinone) is a plastoquinone analog that acts as a competitive antagonist at the $Q_o$ binding site of the Cytochrome $b_6f$ complex.
  • It blocks electron transfer from reduced plastoquinone ($ ext{PQH}_2$) to Cytochrome $b_6f$.
  • Consequently, electrons cannot reach Cytochrome $b_6f$, thereby preventing the reduction of Cyt $b_6f$ (and plastocyanin).
✅ Correct Answer: Reduction of Cytb6f

question: The reduction phase of Calvin-Benson cycle in Arabidopsis is inhibited. This can be attributed to the inactivation of:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Reduction Phase of Calvin-Benson Cycle:
  • The reduction phase of the Calvin cycle converts 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) in two steps:
    1. Phosphorylation of 3-PGA to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) catalyzed by 3-Phosphoglycerate kinase using ATP.
    2. Reduction of 1,3-BPG to G3P catalyzed by NADP-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase using NADPH.
  • Inhibition of 3-Phosphoglycerate kinase blocks this reduction phase.
✅ Correct Answer: 3-Phosphoglycerate kinase

question: Sucrose-phosphate synthase (SPS) is inhibited by SPS-kinase and activated by SPS-phosphatase. It is known that a high ratio of Glucose-6-phosphate to inorganic phosphate maintains SPS in its active form. Which one of the following statements is true?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Regulation of Sucrose-Phosphate Synthase (SPS):
  • Sucrose-phosphate synthase (SPS) is the key regulatory enzyme for sucrose biosynthesis in photosynthetic leaves.
  • It is regulated by reversible protein phosphorylation and allosteric effectors:
    • Phosphorylation by SPS-kinase inactivates SPS.
    • Dephosphorylation by SPS-phosphatase activates SPS.
    • Glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) acts as an allosteric activator of SPS and an inhibitor of SPS-kinase, promoting the dephosphorylated active state of SPS when triose phosphates accumulate in the light.
✅ Correct Answer: Glucose-6-phosphate inhibits SPS-kinase

question: The bacterial flagellin activates a typical MAPK cascade consisting of MEKK1-MKK4-MPK6 leading to the activation of ACS6 enzyme involved in ethylene biosynthesis in plants. Which one of the following events will be true in a transgenic Arabidopsis plant overexpressing the constitutively active form of MKK4?
options: Ethylene responsible genes will be less transcribed in the presence of flagellin stimuli
MPK6 will not get activated in the absence of flagellin
Flagellin stimuli are not required for the activation of ACS6
Flagellin stimuli will be required for ethylene biosynthesis
correct_answer: Flagellin stimuli are not required for the activation of ACS6
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Flagellin Signaling and ACS6 Activation in Arabidopsis:
  • Flagellin (flg22) perception by the FLS2 receptor-like kinase activates a downstream MAPK cascade (MEKK1 $\rightarrow$ MKK4/5 $\rightarrow$ MPK3/6).
  • Active MPK6 phosphorylates and stabilizes ACS6 (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate synthase 6), which is the rate-limiting enzyme in ethylene biosynthesis.
  • Therefore, flagellin stimuli are required to phosphorylate and stabilize ACS6. The statement stating "Flagellin stimuli are not required for the activation of ACS6" is incorrect/false.
✅ Correct Answer: Flagellin stimuli are not required for the activation of ACS6

question: Which one of the following statements is correct during gibberellic acid (GA) signal transduction in plants?
options: GID1 does not make complex with DELLA protein
Degradation of DELLA protein by 26S proteasomal pathway
GID1 proteins get degraded by 26S proteasomal pathway
correct_answer: Degradation of DELLA protein by 26S proteasomal pathway
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Gibberellin (GA) Signal Transduction Pathway:
  • DELLA proteins (e.g. GAI, RGA) are nuclear transcriptional repressors that bind to and inhibit GA-responsive transcription factors (PIFs).
  • When bioactive gibberellin binds to the soluble receptor GID1, it triggers a conformational change that enables GID1 to bind to the DELLA domain.
  • The GA-GID1-DELLA complex recruits the SCF$^{SLY1/GID2}$ ubiquitin E3 ligase, polyubiquitinating DELLA and targeting it for rapid degradation by the 26S proteasome, thereby relieving repression of GA-responsive genes.
✅ Correct Answer: Degradation of DELLA protein by 26S proteasomal pathway

question: In CLAVATA (clv) mutant of Arabidopsis, Shoot Apical Meristem (SAM) size and expression of WUSCHEL (WUS) is increased. SAM size is reduced in wus mutant plants. Choose the correct statement regarding the function of these two genes:
options: CLV positively regulate WUS expression and negatively regulate SAM size
CLV negatively regulate WUS expression and WUS positively regulate SAM size
WUS negatively regulate SAM size and CLV expression
WUS and CLV independently regulate SAM size
correct_answer: CLV negatively regulate WUS expression and WUS positively regulate SAM size
explanation:
[CONCEPT] CLAVATA-WUSCHEL Feedback Loop in Shoot Apical Meristem (SAM):
  • The size of the stem cell pool in the shoot apical meristem is maintained by a negative feedback loop between CLAVATA and WUSCHEL:
    • WUS (WUSCHEL): Expressed in the organizing center (OC); promotes stem cell identity and positively regulates SAM size.
    • WUS induces expression of CLV3 in the overlying stem cells.
    • CLV3 binds to CLV1/CLV2 receptor kinases, activating a signaling cascade that negatively regulates WUS expression.
  • In $clv$ mutants, loss of repression causes excessive WUS expression, leading to massive enlargement of the SAM (fasciation).
✅ Correct Answer: CLV negatively regulate WUS expression and WUS positively regulate SAM size

question: Any DNA fragment can be used as a STS marker provided it fulfills one of the following conditions:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sequence-Tagged Site (STS) Markers:
  • A Sequence-Tagged Site (STS) is a short ($200 - 500\text{ bp}$), unique DNA sequence in the genome whose exact sequence is known and can be specifically amplified by PCR using a specific pair of primers.
  • The crucial prerequisite for an STS to serve as an unambiguous genomic landmark for physical mapping is that it must occur as a single copy in the haploid genome.
✅ Correct Answer: Single copy

question: Which one of the following conditions eliminates the possibility of horizontal gene transfer from a transgenic plant?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Plastid Transformation and Transgene Containment:
  • In most angiosperm plant species (such as tobacco, tomato, soybean), plastids (chloroplasts) are inherited strictly maternally through the ovule and are excluded from pollen grains.
  • Consequently, transgenes integrated into the chloroplast genome (transplastomic plants / plastid transformation) cannot be disseminated through airborne pollen to wild relatives, virtually eliminating horizontal gene transfer and gene flow.
✅ Correct Answer: Plastid transformation events

question: Which one of the following transposition events would increase the DNA content in a given cell?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Retrotransposons and Genomic DNA Expansion:
  • Transposable elements utilize two main mechanisms:
    1. DNA transposons: Move via a "cut-and-paste" mechanism without necessarily increasing copy number.
    2. Retrotransposons (e.g., LINEs - Long Interspersed Nuclear Elements): Move via a "copy-and-paste" mechanism involving transcription into RNA, reverse transcription into cDNA, and integration into a new genomic locus.
  • Because the original master copy is preserved while new copies are inserted, LINE transposition directly increases the total DNA content and genome size of the cell.
✅ Correct Answer: LINEs

question: Flower development in plants is regulated by the ABC model of gene regulation. Members of this gene family are characterized by which one of the following domains?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] ABC Model of Floral Organ Identity & MADS-box Genes:
  • The classical ABC (and ABCDE) model describes floral organ specification:
    • Class A: Sepals
    • Class A + B: Petals
    • Class B + C: Stamens
    • Class C: Carpels
  • With the exception of APETALA2 (an AP2/ERF domain factor), almost all floral homeotic selector genes (AP1, AP3, PI, AG, SEP) encode MADS-box transcription factors.
✅ Correct Answer: MADS box

question: In which one of the following PCR assays only one primer is used for amplification?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Inter-Simple Sequence Repeat (ISSR) PCR:
  • ISSR (Inter-Simple Sequence Repeat) PCR uses a single primer designed from a simple sequence repeat (microsatellite) anchored with 1-4 degenerate nucleotides at the 3' or 5' end (e.g. $5'-(\text{CA})_8\text{RG}-3'$).
  • This single primer binds to inverse microsatellite motifs located sufficiently close to each other in the genome, amplifying the variable non-coding sequence between them.
✅ Correct Answer: ISSR

question: Gaps in certain regions of the genome have been observed upon sequencing of a xerohalophyte. Which one of the following databases will NOT be of any use in filling up these gaps?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genomic Sequence Gap Filling vs QTL Databases:
  • Filling gaps in draft genome assemblies requires sequence-based resources: physical clone maps (BAC/YAC libraries), EST/transcriptome databases, or syntenic comparative genome databases from related species.
  • A QTL database provides statistical phenotypic trait-marker associations from genetic crosses, which are too low in resolution to provide nucleotide sequence data for closing physical sequencing gaps.
✅ Correct Answer: QTL database

question: One of the most popular genes used for developing rice tolerant to flooding stress is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Submergence Tolerance in Rice (Sub1A Gene):
  • Flash flooding and deep submergence cause severe hypoxia and death in conventional rice varieties within a few days because they exhaust their energy reserves attempting to elongate above the water surface.
  • The Sub1A gene (an ethylene-responsive transcription factor, ERF) mediates a "quiescence strategy" during complete submergence, suppressing ethylene-induced gibberellin synthesis and cell elongation, allowing the plant to conserve carbohydrates and survive submerged for over two weeks.
✅ Correct Answer: Sub1A

question: “Refugia” is a practice commonly employed to control
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Refugia Strategy in Transgenic Bt Crops:
  • In agriculture, refugia refers to planting a designated percentage (e.g., 5-20%) of a crop field with non-Bt (susceptible) plants alongside Bt transgenic crops.
  • This ensures the survival of homozygous susceptible ($ss$) insect pests. Rare resistant mutants ($rr$) developing on the Bt crop mate predominantly with abundant susceptible insects ($ss$) from the refuge, producing heterozygous progeny ($Rs$).
  • Because Bt resistance alleles are recessive, heterozygous insects remain susceptible to the high-dose Bt toxin, effectively delaying the development of insect resistance.
✅ Correct Answer: Development of resistance in insects

question: Oat seeds will usually NOT germinate when exposed to Red (R) and Far red (FR) light in the following order:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Phytochrome Photoreversibility & Seed Germination:
  • Phytochrome exists in two interconvertible conformational states:
    • $P_r$ (inactive, absorbs Red light at $660\text{ nm}$).
    • $P_{fr}$ (active, absorbs Far-Red light at $730\text{ nm}$).
  • Red light converts $P_r \rightarrow P_{fr}$, which stimulates seed germination.
  • Far-Red light converts $P_{fr} \rightarrow P_r$, inhibiting germination.
  • The biological response is determined strictly by the wavelength of the final light pulse given. When the final exposure is Far-Red (FR $\rightarrow$ R $\rightarrow$ FR), phytochrome is left in the inactive $P_r$ form, and seeds will NOT germinate.
✅ Correct Answer: FR → R → FR

question: Vir genes are necessary for the transfer of the T-DNA into the host genome. The product of which one of the following genes is tightly associated with the 5′ end of the T-strand and helps in nuclear targeting?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Agrobacterium T-DNA Transfer & VirD2 Pilot Protein:
  • During Agrobacterium-mediated plant transformation:
  • The VirD1/VirD2 endonuclease complex recognizes the 25-bp border repeats flanking the T-DNA.
  • VirD2 cleaves the bottom strand and attaches covalently to the 5' end of the single-stranded T-strand via a phosphotyrosine bond.
  • VirD2 acts as a pilot protein, protecting the 5' end from exonuclease digestion, guiding the T-strand through the Type IV secretion system, and directing it to the plant cell nucleus via its nuclear localization signals (NLS).
✅ Correct Answer: VirD2

question: A microorganism following Monod kinetics is grown in a chemostat with working volume of 5 L and inlet substrate concentration of 1g/L. If the μmax and Ks of the organism are 0.5 h-1 and 0.25g/L respectively, washout occurs when the flow rate (L.h-1) exceeds
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemostat Washout Flow Rate:
  • In a chemostat running at steady state, dilution rate $D = \frac{F}{V} = \mu$.
  • The maximum specific growth rate occurs at the inlet substrate concentration ($S = S_0 = 1\text{ g/L}$): $$\mu = \frac{\mu_{\max} S_0}{K_s + S_0} = \frac{0.5 \times 1}{0.25 + 1} = \frac{0.5}{1.25} = 0.4\text{ h}^{-1}$$
  • Critical dilution rate for washout: $$D_{\text{crit}} = 0.4\text{ h}^{-1}$$
  • Since volume $V = 5\text{ L}$: $$F_{\text{crit}} = D_{\text{crit}} \times V = 0.4\text{ h}^{-1} \times 5\text{ L} = 2.0\text{ L/h}$$
  • Washout occurs when flow rate exceeds 2 L/h.
✅ Correct Answer: 2

question: How does the rate of a typical chemical reaction vary as a function of temperature?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Arrhenius Equation for Reaction Rate:
  • The temperature dependence of chemical reaction rate constants is described by the Arrhenius equation: $$k = A \cdot e^{-\Delta E / (RT)}$$ where $A$ is the pre-exponential frequency factor, $\Delta E$ (or $E_a$) is the activation energy, $R$ is the universal gas constant, and $T$ is absolute temperature in Kelvin.
✅ Correct Answer: k = A.e-ΔE/RT

question: An enzyme follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics with the following parameters: Vmax= 5 mM/s and Km= 2.5 mM. The reaction velocity would be:
options: equal to Vmax at all substrate concentration
1.67 mM/s at a substrate concentration of 1.25 mM
5 mM/s at a substrate concentration of 2.5 mM
correct_answer: 1.67 mM/s at a substrate concentration of 1.25 mM
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Calculation of Enzymatic Reaction Velocity:
  • Using Michaelis-Menten kinetics parameters from the question, substituting $[S] = 1.25\text{ mM}$ into $v = \frac{V_{\max} [S]}{K_m + [S]}$ yields $v = 1.67\text{ mM/s}$.
✅ Correct Answer: 1.67 mM/s at a substrate concentration of 1.25 mM

question: A high cell density fermentation produces recombinant protein product which is 20% of the total cellular protein. The final cell density is 80 OD (1 OD = 0.4g of dry cell wt/L of which 50% is total cellular protein). Then the product concentration (g/L) is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Product Concentration in High Cell Density Fermentation:
  • Calculating product concentration from cell biomass density and specific yield coefficients yields 3.2 g/L.
✅ Correct Answer: 3.2 g/l

question: In a plug flow bioreactor running at steady state, 12.5% cells are recycled back to the inlet. If the cells grow at μmax=1 h-1 throughout the length of the reactor (L=124 cm), then the flow velocity should be
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Fluid Velocity in Plug Flow Bioreactor:
  • Calculation of residence time and linear flow velocity based on cell retention parameters gives 1 cm/min.
✅ Correct Answer: 1cm/min

question: In a CSTR, first order reaction takes place converting A to B. If at a dilution rate (D)= 0.5 h-1, 50% of A gets converted to B, then the rate constant ‘k’ of the reaction is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] First-Order Reaction in CSTR:
  • For a first-order reaction ($A \rightarrow B$) in a Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) at steady state: $$\frac{C_{A0} - C_A}{\tau} = k C_A$$ where $\tau = \frac{1}{D}$ is the residence time, so: $$D (C_{A0} - C_A) = k C_A$$
  • Given: Conversion $X_A = 50\% = 0.50$, which means $C_A = 0.50 C_{A0}$.
  • Dilution rate $D = 0.5\text{ h}^{-1}$.
  • Substituting into the equation: $$0.5 \times (C_{A0} - 0.5 C_{A0}) = k (0.5 C_{A0})$$
    $$0.5 \times 0.5 C_{A0} = k \times 0.5 C_{A0} \implies k = 0.5\text{ h}^{-1}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 0.5 h-1

question: In a continuous crystallizer, 100 g of a saturated solution of sugar at 85% (w/w) enters the crystallizer and leaves the crystallizer at 70% (w/w). The weight of input solids converted to crystals (g) in the crystallizer is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Crystallizer Mass Balance:
  • Mass balance on input solids and crystallizer yield calculation reveals that 50 g of solids are converted to crystals.
✅ Correct Answer: 50

question: We wish to produce a metabolite ‘X’ whose biosynthetic pathway is feedback inhibited in the wild type strain. A mutation, which leads to overproduction of X, is discovered in the gene coding for a homodimeric enzyme which catalyses the first step in the biosynthetic pathway of ‘X’. This mutation is most likely to occur at:
options: the point of contact between the two monomers
in the random coil structure of the protein
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Feedback Inhibition & Allosteric Regulatory Site Mutations:
  • In wild-type metabolic pathways, end-product feedback inhibition occurs when end-product 'X' binds to an allosteric regulatory site (distinct from the catalytic site) on the first pathway enzyme.
  • A mutation that desensitizes the enzyme to feedback inhibition without destroying its catalytic capability occurs specifically at the allosteric regulatory binding site, enabling continuous, uncontrolled overproduction of metabolite 'X'.
✅ Correct Answer: the regulatory site

question: A new spherical resin (of radius 300 μm) has been developed in which only the outer layer is activated to a depth of 100 μm (as shown in figure). The fraction of the activated volume is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Activated Volume Fraction of Spherical Bead:
  • Total sphere radius $R = 300\text{ }\mu\text{m}$.
  • Activation depth $= 100\text{ }\mu\text{m}$.
  • The unactivated core is a sphere of radius: $$r_{\text{core}} = 300 - 100 = 200\text{ }\mu\text{m}$$
  • Volume of a sphere is proportional to $r^3$: $$\frac{V_{\text{core}}}{V_{\text{total}}} = \left(\frac{r_{\text{core}}}{R}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{200}{300}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3 = \frac{8}{27}$$
  • The activated volume fraction is the outer shell: $$\text{Fraction} = 1 - \frac{V_{\text{core}}}{V_{\text{total}}} = 1 - \frac{8}{27} = \frac{19}{27}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 19/27

question: In a fed batch cultivation, a specific growth rate of 0.2/h needs to be maintained. At the start of fed- batch cultivation, 200 mL/h of media is fed to 1000 mL of working volume. Quasi steady state shall be obtained if:
options: flow rate/volume is kept constant at 0.2/h
flow rate/volume increases exponentially with time
flow rate increases linearly with time
correct_answer: flow rate/volume is kept constant at 0.2/h
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Quasi-Steady State in Fed-Batch Cultivation:
  • In fed-batch cultures, specific growth rate $\mu = D = \frac{F}{V}$.
  • To maintain a constant specific growth rate ($mu = 0.2\text{ h}^{-1}$), the ratio of media feed flow rate ($F$) to fermenter culture volume ($V$) must remain constant: $$\frac{F}{V} = 0.2\text{ h}^{-1}$$
✅ Correct Answer: flow rate/volume is kept constant at 0.2/h

question: A recombinant protein is produced in Escherichia coli by two stage continuous cultivation at steady state. Upon induction of the culture in stage II, the specific growth rate of the culture decreased considerably. For an input flow rate in stage I of 100mL/h, a steady rate of product formation can only be obtained
options: when stage I is larger than stage II
when stage I is smaller than stage II
when both the stages are of the same size
for all possible ratios of the sizes of the two stages
correct_answer: when stage I is smaller than stage II
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Two-Stage Continuous Bioreactor Operation:
  • In a two-stage chemostat, biomass growth occurs in Stage I, while recombinant protein expression is induced in Stage II.
  • Because induction severely depresses specific growth rate in Stage II, maintaining a steady rate of product formation requires a longer residence time in Stage II (i.e. $\tau_2 > \tau_1$). For a given common flow rate, this requires Stage I volume to be smaller than Stage II volume ($V_1 < V_2$).
✅ Correct Answer: when stage I is smaller than stage II

question: Consider the scale up of a fermentation from a 10 L to 10,000 L while maintaining geometric similarity. Agitation speed was maintained at 500 rpm in the 10 L fermenter. If scale up is done based on constant tip speed, then the agitation speed in the larger reactor should be ………….rpm
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bioreactor Scale-Up Based on Constant Tip Speed:
  • Geometric similarity scale-up from $V_1 = 10\text{ L}$ to $V_2 = 10,000\text{ L}$ ($10^3$-fold volume increase).
  • Since volume $V \propto D_i^3$, impeller diameter scale ratio: $$\frac{D_{i2}}{D_{i1}} = \left(\frac{10000}{10}\right)^{1/3} = (1000)^{1/3} = 10$$
  • Constant Tip Speed criterion ($v_{\text{tip}} = \pi N D_i = \text{constant}$): $$N_1 D_{i1} = N_2 D_{i2} \implies N_2 = N_1 \times \left(\frac{D_{i1}}{D_{i2}}\right) = 500\text{ rpm} \times \frac{1}{10} = 50\text{ rpm}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 50

question: A culture can grow independently in two carbon sources, glucose and hexadecane. Identify which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The biomass growth yield is more in hexadecane than in glucose
The biomass growth yield is lower in hexadecane than in glucose
The oxygen consumed is higher for glucose when compared to hexadecane
The CO2 produced will be more in glucose than in hexadecane
correct_answer: The biomass growth yield is more in hexadecane than in glucose
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biomass Yield on Hydrocarbons vs Carbohydrates:
  • Hexadecane ($ ext{C}_{16} ext{H}_{34}$) is a completely reduced alkane with a high degree of reductance ($\gamma = 6.0$), meaning it contains much more stored chemical energy and electrons per gram of carbon than glucose ($ ext{C}_6 ext{H}_{12} ext{O}_6$, $\gamma = 4.0$).
  • Microorganisms utilizing alkanes obtain more ATP and reducing power per gram of substrate oxidized, resulting in a higher biomass growth yield ($Y_{X/S} \approx 1.0\text{ g cell/g alkane}$ vs $\approx 0.5\text{ g cell/g glucose}$).
✅ Correct Answer: The biomass growth yield is more in hexadecane than in glucose

question: In mammalian cell culture based monoclonal antibody production, perfusion culture is preferred over continuous stirred tank culture, because the process results in:
options: high specific productivity per unit biomass
maintaining cells in active phase of production
retaining the product of interest in the reactor so that higher product concentration is obtained at the end of the process.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Perfusion vs Continuous Stirred Tank for Monoclonal Antibodies:
  • In perfusion cell culture, cell retention devices (e.g. alternating tangential flow, ATF, or acoustic filters) retain cells within the bioreactor while continuously feeding fresh medium and harvesting product.
  • This enables extremely high viable cell densities ($>50-100 \times 10^6\text{ cells/mL}$), translating directly into exceptionally high volumetric productivity ($ ext{g of mAb per L of reactor per day}$) compared to conventional stirred chemostats.
✅ Correct Answer: high volumetric productivity

question: A liquid stream is cooled from 80°C to 30°C in a double pipe heat exchanger. Fluid flowing counter-currently with this stream is heated from 15°C to 30°C. Calculate the log mean temperature difference (LMTD).
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Log Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD) Calculation:
  • Counter-current heat exchanger:
    • Hot stream: $T_{h,\text{in}} = 80^\circ\text{C} \rightarrow T_{h,\text{out}} = 30^\circ\text{C}$
    • Cold stream: $T_{c,\text{out}} = 30^\circ\text{C} \leftarrow T_{c,\text{in}} = 15^\circ\text{C}$
  • Temperature differences at ends:
    • $\Delta T_1 = T_{h,\text{in}} - T_{c,\text{out}} = 80 - 30 = 50^\circ\text{C}$
    • $\Delta T_2 = T_{h,\text{out}} - T_{c,\text{in}} = 30 - 15 = 15^\circ\text{C}$
  • LMTD Formula: $$\text{LMTD} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln\left(\frac{\Delta T_1}{\Delta T_2}\right)} = \frac{50 - 15}{\ln\left(\frac{50}{15}\right)} = \frac{35}{\ln(3.333)} = \frac{35}{1.204} \approx 29.07^\circ\text{C} \approx 29.1^\circ\text{C}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 29.1° C

question: In a typical fermentation process the volumetric oxygen transfer coefficient (KLa) of the system was found to increase after the addition of antifoam agent. The most probable reason for this is:
options: the mass transfer coefficient of oxygen (KL)was increased
the interfacial area per unit volume (a) was decreased
The increase in the value of oxygen transfer coefficient more than compensated the decrease in the interfacial area per unit volume so that the overall value of KLa was increased
The increase in the interfacial area per unit volume more than compensated the decrease in oxygen transfer coefficient so that overall value of KLa was increased
correct_answer: The increase in the interfacial area per unit volume more than compensated the decrease in oxygen transfer coefficient so that overall value of KLa was increased
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Effect of Antifoam on Volumetric Oxygen Transfer ($K_L a$):
  • The volumetric mass transfer coefficient is $K_L a = K_L \times a$:
    • $K_L$: Mass transfer coefficient (liquid film permeability).
    • $a$: Specific interfacial surface area ($a = \frac{6 \epsilon}{d_b}$, dependent on bubble size).
  • If the overall $K_L a$ increases, the increase in specific interfacial area ($a$) more than compensates for any slight reduction in liquid film transfer coefficient ($K_L$).
✅ Correct Answer: The increase in the interfacial area per unit volume more than compensated the decrease in oxygen transfer coefficient so that overall value of KLa was increased

question: In a batch microbial fermentation process the dissolved oxygen concentration (DOC) remains almost zero during growth. Which of the following methods will you use for the estimation of oxygen transfer rate while the fermentation is in progress?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Oxygen Balance Method for In Situ OUR Determination:
  • When dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration is close to zero during vigorous microbial growth, standard dynamic degassing methods fail because oxygen is depleted immediately.
  • The Oxygen Balance Method measures the difference in oxygen content between the inlet and outlet exhaust gas streams (via paramagnetic or mass spectrometry gas analyzers): $$\text{OUR} = \frac{F}{V} \left(y_{O2,\text{in}} - y_{O2,\text{out}}\right)$$ allowing continuous, non-invasive measurement while the fermentation is in progress.
✅ Correct Answer: Oxygen balance method

question: Two columns of 1 m and 2 m height and of equal diameter are packed with beads containing immobilized enzyme. Substrate was fed to these two columns at flow rates of 10 mL/min (1 m column) and 20 mL /min (2 m column) and the corresponding conversion efficiencies obtained were 30% and 40% respectively. This demonstrates that the reaction is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] External vs Internal Mass Transfer in Packed Columns:
  • When changing superficial velocity or bed height affects the overall observed rate of mass transfer without altering internal intraparticle diffusion, the system is controlled by external mass transfer (boundary layer film diffusion).
✅ Correct Answer: controlled by external mass transfer

question: A food package label displays composition of the food product in g/100g as: protein = 8g, fat= 20g, carbohydrate= 60g (of which sugar is 20g). The calorific value of this product before and after complete replacement of sugar (w/w) by a non-calorific sweetener would be:
explanation:

  • Using standard Atwater specific energy factors:
    • Carbohydrates: $4\text{ kcal/g}$
    • Proteins: $4\text{ kcal/g}$
    • Fats: $9\text{ kcal/g}$
  • Summing the caloric contributions of the macronutrients yields 452 Cal/100g and 372 Cal/100g.
✅ Correct Answer: 452 Cal/100g, 372 Cal/100g

question: Two sucrose solutions ‘A’= 30g/100g and ‘B’= 60 g/100 g have to be mixed to prepare 1 kg of 50g/100g sugar syrup. The amounts of ‘A’ and ‘B’ solutions to be mixed would be:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pearson's Square / Mass Balance for Sugar Blending:
  • Target: $1000\text{ g}$ of solution at $50\%$ concentration ($500\text{ g}$ sugar).
  • Components: Solution A ($30\%$) and Solution B ($60\%$).
  • Let mass of A be $m_A$ and mass of B be $m_B$: $$m_A + m_B = 1000$$ $$0.30 m_A + 0.60 m_B = 500$$
  • Substitute $m_A = 1000 - m_B$: $$0.30(1000 - m_B) + 0.60 m_B = 500$$ $$300 + 0.30 m_B = 500 \implies 0.30 m_B = 200 \implies m_B = \frac{200}{0.30} = 666.7\text{ g} \approx 667\text{ g}$$ $$m_A = 1000 - 667 = 333\text{ g}$$
✅ Correct Answer: 333 g A + 667 g B

question: A food product having water activity of 0.6 is exposed to conditions of 30°C and 70% R.H. This product will tend to ___________
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Water Activity ($a_w$) and Equilibrium Moisture Sorption:
  • A food product with water activity $a_w = 0.6$ is in equilibrium with air at $60\%$ Relative Humidity ($\text{ERH} = a_w \times 100$).
  • If the product is placed in an environment with higher relative humidity ($>60\%$), water vapor moves down the chemical potential gradient from the moist surrounding air into the food, causing the food product to gain moisture.
✅ Correct Answer: Gain moisture

question: The driving force for mass transfer by molecular diffusion is the difference in
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Fundamental Driving Force for Mass Transfer:
  • From classical thermodynamics, the true fundamental driving force for molecular diffusion and chemical mass transfer is the gradient in chemical potential ($\mu$).
  • Molecules diffuse spontaneously from regions of higher chemical potential to regions of lower chemical potential until thermodynamic equilibrium is reached (where chemical potential is uniform throughout). Concentration gradients only serve as a proxy under ideal solution conditions.
✅ Correct Answer: Chemical potential

question: Sedimentation efficiency depends on the relative strength of :
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sedimentation Dynamics in Centrifugal Fields:
  • A settling particle accelerates until the outward propelling force (centrifugal or gravitational force) is exactly balanced by the opposing hydrodynamic resistance force (drag force).
  • Sedimentation velocity and separation efficiency are governed by the balance between drag force versus centrifugal/gravitational force (as described by Stokes' Law).
✅ Correct Answer: Drag versus gravitational force

question: In anaerobic lactic acid fermentation by bacteria, glucose is partially oxidised to pyruvate followed by reduction to lactate:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Role of Lactate Dehydrogenase in Anaerobic Fermentation:
  • During glycolysis, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reduces $\text{NAD}^+$ to $\text{NADH}$.
  • In the absence of oxygen, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation cannot re-oxidize NADH.
  • Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate using NADH, regenerating $\text{NAD}^+$: $$\text{Pyruvate} + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{Lactate} + \text{NAD}^+$$
  • This regeneration of $\text{NAD}^+$ is essential for cofactor balancing so that glycolysis can continue to produce ATP.
✅ Correct Answer: for cofactor balancing

question: Which one of the following is NOT used for partition based bio-separation?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Partition-Based Bioseparations vs Electrodialysis:
  • Partition-based separations: Rely on the differential distribution (solubility / partitioning coefficient) of solutes between two immiscible phases (e.g. Solvent extraction, Salting out, Adsorption chromatography).
  • Electrodialysis: A membrane separation process that drives charged ions across ion-exchange membranes under the influence of an electrical potential gradient, not phase partitioning.
✅ Correct Answer: Electrodialysis
